In C++, there isn't a de-facto standard logging tool.  In my experience, shops roll their own.  This creates a bit of a problem, however, when trying to create reusable software components.  If everything in your system depends on the logging component, this makes the software less reusable, basically forcing any downstream projects to take your logging framework along with the components they really want.  

IOC (dependency injection) doesn't really help with the problem since your components would need to depend on a logging abstraction.  Logging components themselves can add dependencies on file I/O, triggering mechanisms, and other possibly unwanted dependencies.  

Does adding a dependency to your proprietary logging framework sacrifice the reusability of the component?

In general, adding a dependency to a proprietary logging framework can make the component less reusable, as it forces downstream projects to use the same logging framework. This can create compatibility issues and make it harder to use the component in different environments.

However, if the logging framework is well-designed and provides a clear and consistent interface for logging, it can also make the component more flexible and easier to use in different environments. It's important to consider the specific requirements of the project and the potential benefits and drawbacks of using a proprietary logging framework.

In some cases, it may be more beneficial to use a third-party logging framework that is widely used and well-documented, such as the Boost.Log library. This can provide a consistent and standardized logging interface that can be easily used across different projects and environments.

Overall, the decision on whether to use a proprietary logging framework or a third-party logging framework depends on the specific requirements of the project and the preferences of the development team.
